design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021240014; PRISMA reporting) of original studies other than case reports that gave the precise location of cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions (CIMDL) in people who snorted cocaine recreationally. Five databases (MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov) were searched on 4 March 2021 by the text and Table 1 (on 1 December 2020 by the PRISMA figure), in five languages. 17 retrospective case series published 1989 to 2020 were included, with 127 people with CIMDL among 282 participants. The share of people with each site damaged was obtained by adding patients across the series, and a four-grade location-based classification was built from those shares: grade 1 septum; grade 2a inferior turbinate and medial maxillary sinus wall, grade 2b palate; grade 3 ethmoid and middle or superior turbinate; grade 4 lamina papyracea, orbit or skull base.
can_establish: How often each part of the nose, palate, orbit and skull base was reported as damaged among the 127 people described in 17 published case series of cocaine-related midline lesions, most of them selected for a particular site or presentation, and how rarely those series report the amount, frequency or stopping of cocaine use.
cannot_establish: How often snorting cocaine damages the nose (no denominator of people who snort cocaine); whether damage spreads in the order the grades assume (no follow-up data: the grades come from counts at one time); whether amount, duration or stopping changes the damage (too sparsely reported to analyse); or whether lesions stop or heal after stopping (no included series followed people after they stopped).

sample.recruitment: Database search on 4 March 2021 (MEDLINE 991 records, Embase 2083, Web of Science 944, Cochrane Library 110, ClinicalTrials.gov 5; Table 1, p. 3259) for studies in English, Italian, German, French or Spanish; reference lists of reviews were hand-checked and added nothing (pp. 3258–3259). The included series were selected by their own authors: 12 of 17 (75 of the 127 people) studied a particular subgroup: a vasculitis-like presentation (4 series), palatal perforation, septal perforation, nasolacrimal duct obstruction with septal perforation, osteocartilaginous necrosis, IgG4 positivity, ANCA or IgG4 positivity, need for surgical management, or nasal deformity (Table 2, p. 3261; editors' count). The review's text describes most series as focused on particular lesion sites, most often the palate, or on vasculitis-like presentations with difficult differential diagnosis (p. 3259).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: any original study of CIMDL in humans, as defined by Trimarchi et al., describing lesions related to recreational intranasal cocaine use with precise location within the sinonasal tract; no minimum number of participants (p. 3258, Methods › Search strategy, 3rd and 4th paragraphs). PICOS: people who snort cocaine recreationally and have CIMDL; localisation by clinical examination, endoscopy or imaging; no comparison; original studies of any kind except case reports and meta-analyses (p. 3259). Excluded: meta-analyses, systematic and narrative reviews, case reports (because they tend to describe only extreme cases, p. 3266), non-human studies and other languages (Fig. 1, p. 3260).
sample.demographics: 61 men and 44 women; sex not extractable for the CIMDL subgroup in two series (22 people). Ages 22 to 66 years, most often in the third or fourth decade by the results text (p. 3259) and in their thirties or forties by the discussion (p. 3265). One series did not report age for its CIMDL subgroup (Table 2, p. 3261). Countries and settings of the series are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Most series gave little or no follow-up; only one series (Trimarchi et al., 2003) gave sparse information on progression over time (pp. 3259, 3265).
sample.selection_effects: Every denominator is people already diagnosed with CIMDL in published series, not people who snort cocaine. By the review's own description most series selected people by lesion site (most often the palate) or by a vasculitis-like presentation, and many were non-consecutive (p. 3259). With case reports excluded as well, the site shares depend on which kinds of series were published. Three series (53 of 127 people) come from one group (Trimarchi et al., 2001, 2003 and 2017) and two from another (Colletti et al., 2013 and 2014); the review does not say whether patients overlap between series from the same group (Tables 2–3).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each series reported. Some figure for duration of cocaine use was given for 11 of 17 series, frequency of use for 2, and whether use was continuing or had stopped for 8 series covering 33 people (Table 3, pp. 3262–3263; editors' count). Exposure to levamisole as an adulterant was reported by a single study (p. 3260).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Intranasal by inclusion. Where reported, duration of use ranged from 2 to 30 years; frequency was given only as once or more a week in one series and twice a week for one person in another (Table 3, pp. 3262–3263).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. The authors name substances mixed into cocaine as a possible confounder they could not account for (p. 3265, Discussion, 6th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Use status when the lesions were described is known for 33 of 127 people: 18 still using and 15 who had stopped (editors' count from Table 3, pp. 3262–3263). Lesions were not compared by status.

comparison.controls: None (PICOS: no comparison available, p. 3259). No people who snort cocaine without lesions and no people with other causes of midline destruction were compared.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name one-sided use, septal deviation or deformity before any use, and the destructive effect of substances mixed into cocaine as confounders that could not be accounted for (p. 3265, Discussion, 6th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Lesion location as each series assessed it: clinical examination, nasal endoscopy, CT or MRI (Table 3, pp. 3262–3263); external-nose deformity where reported (Table 5, p. 3264); surgical pathology where reported (Table 6, p. 3264). Study quality: NHLBI Study Quality Assessment Tools, rated in duplicate, good if at least 80% of items were met, fair 50 to 80%, poor under 50%; level of evidence by the OCEBM scale (p. 3259, Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assessment methods differed between series and are not stated for three series (Table 3). No reliability of lesion assessment is reported for any series.
outcomes.operationalization: A site counted as involved if any series reported it perforated, eroded or destroyed in a person. Sites were grouped into five locations and each was expressed as a share of all 127 people (Table 4, p. 3264). Individual patterns could be reconstructed for 18 people in four series; the other series gave only how many people had each site involved (p. 3260, Results, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: five descriptive shares, no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Abstracts and full texts were reviewed in duplicate, a study going forward at the abstract stage if either rater judged it eligible and full-text disagreements resolved by consensus; quality was rated in duplicate; duplicate data extraction is not stated (pp. 3258–3259).

analysis.effect_sizes: Simple shares of the 127 people, no weighting, no intervals (Table 4, p. 3264): nasal septum 126 (99.2%), grade 1; inferior turbinate or medial maxillary sinus wall 75 (59%), grade 2a; palate 38 (29.9%), grade 2b; ethmoid, middle or superior turbinate 29 (22.8%), grade 3; lamina papyracea, orbit or skull base 10 (7.9%), grade 4. Editors' calculation, Wilson 95% intervals treating the 127 as one sample (which overstates precision, because the series were selected by site and are heterogeneous): 95.7 to 99.9%, 50.4 to 67.2%, 22.6 to 38.4%, 16.4 to 30.9% and 4.3 to 13.9%. External-nose deformity was listed for 10 of 17 series (Table 5): saddle nose in 7 people across 5 series, collapse of the nasal pyramid in 7 people across 2 series, and single cases of destroyed nostrils, nasal ala, columella and philtrum (editors' count; not a rate, since the other series did not report on the external nose).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021240014 (p. 3258). The registered protocol was not among the files read, so the report has not been compared with it; the paper reports no deviation. Whether the classification, the secondary objective, was in the protocol is not stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cocaine-use, external-nose and pathology data were tabulated where available but not related to lesion site or extent, for want of data (p. 3265). The two poor-quality series were kept on the authors' statement that their distribution data agreed with the others; no figures are shown for that check (pp. 3260–3261).
analysis.power: Not applicable. The authors call the sample relatively small and too small to relate demographics to lesion patterns (pp. 3265–3266).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 127 people with cocaine-related midline lesions in 17 retrospective case series, all but one had the septum involved, and fewer had damage further out: inferior turbinate or medial maxillary wall 75, palate 38, ethmoid or middle and superior turbinates 29, orbit or skull base 10. These are counts at one time per person, added across series that mostly selected people by site or presentation. Cocaine-use data were too sparse to analyse, external-nose deformity and pathology were reported inconsistently, and no series followed people after they stopped using.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion say a specific prevalence pattern was found and propose a four-grade classification; the discussion calls it a “simpler and progression-based classification” (p. 3265) and hypothesises that the decreasing shares mimic the natural course, with the septum as the starting point (p. 3265). Gaps: (1) the order of spread is inferred from how many people had each site involved at one time, not from following anyone; the authors say validation needs longitudinal data and that only one series has sparse data of that kind (pp. 3265–3266). (2) The abstract (p. 3257) and results text (p. 3260) give 59% to the nasal floor and 29.9% to the inferolateral nasal wall, while Table 4 and Fig. 2 give 59% to the inferior turbinate and medial maxillary wall and 29.9% to the palate, so a reader of the abstract alone gets the palate share wrong. (3) 12 of 17 series selected people by site or presentation, yet the review states that no significant biases towards its objectives were identified (p. 3259) and never discusses how this selection shapes the shares. (4) The suggestion that the lack of follow-up data may be partly due to stigma, with late presentation and loss to follow-up as its consequences (p. 3265), rests on one citation (ref. 28, a paper on the global burden of mental and addictive disorders by its title) and gives no follow-up figures. The conclusion's own caveats (small sample; prospective studies needed) are accurate.

timeline.event: Trimarchi et al.: 18 people with CIMDL compared with 21 with Wegener granulomatosis at one Italian department; the largest contributor of detailed lesion data to this review (ref. 10)
Trimarchi, Nicolai, Lombardi et al. (Am J Rhinol 17:33–43): 25 people; the only included series with some data on progression over time (ref. 26, as described in this review; not read).
Westreich and Lawson: the earlier location-based scoring of midline necrotizing lesions, which this review judges too detailed and without prognostic value (ref. 11, as described; not read).
Young-IFOS consensus led partly by this review's first and senior authors adopts this classification (statement 2.2, consensus, mean 8.44) and bases its management scheme on it

replication.where_it_stands: The systematic review of where these lesions lie, by its authors' account the first; its classification has been adopted by a 2025 expert consensus with overlapping authors (Saibene et al., 2025), which cites no study validating the grades as stages. No longitudinal study of lesions after people stop using cocaine appears in either paper.

funding.funder: The authors received no funding for this work (p. 3266).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest pertaining to this work (p. 3266).
funding.affiliations_note: Otolaryngology and maxillofacial surgery units of Santi Paolo e Carlo Hospital, University of Milan; San Luigi Gonzaga University Hospital, University of Turin; and the Italian Study Group on Odontogenic Sinusitis (p. 3257). One review author (F. Allevi) is a co-author of an included series (Colletti et al., 2013, ref. 19, by the reference list, p. 3267); the review does not say how that series was rated or extracted. The first and senior authors (L. Nitro, A. M. Saibene) later helped lead the 2025 consensus that adopted the classification. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people with cocaine-related nasal lesions (and, ideally, of people who snort cocaine before any lesion), examined by endoscopy and CT at set intervals with cocaine use measured and checked by toxicology, would show whether lesions spread in the proposed order, how fast, and whether they stop, shrink or heal after use stops; a count of lesions among people who snort cocaine in the community would supply the missing denominator.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: PICOS stated (p. 3259): people who snort cocaine recreationally with CIMDL; localisation of lesions; no comparison; localisation and extent; original studies except case reports and meta-analyses.

Registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021240014, p. 3258), but the paper neither dates the registration against the search (whose date it gives inconsistently) nor reports deviations, and the protocol was not among the files read.
Case reports excluded with a reason: they tend to describe only extreme cases and would bias the overall picture (p. 3266).

Five databases including a trial registry, full search strings in Table 1, hand-checked review reference lists, and a search within 24 months of publication; but the restriction to five languages is not justified (8 records were excluded for language, Fig. 1), no grey literature or experts were consulted, and reference lists of the included studies are not said to have been searched. Judged 'no' by AMSTAR 2 item 4 as written (publication restrictions must be justified for partial yes), as the project applies it (decision p-amstar2-item4, the senior author's to settle).
Abstracts and full texts reviewed in duplicate by different authors; inclusive at the abstract stage, consensus at full text (p. 3258).
Quality rating was done in duplicate, but data extraction is described without any second extractor or check (p. 3259).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives counts for seven reasons among the 173 full texts excluded; no list of excluded studies appears and no supplement is mentioned.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2 and 3 give design, quality, numbers, sex, age, subgroup selected, assessment method, lesions and what was known of cocaine use; country, setting, period and follow-up of each series are not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: NHLBI tool applied in duplicate, with the main shortfalls named (comparability of patients, little follow-up, non-consecutive series; p. 3259), but only a summary rating per study is shown (Table 2), not item-level judgments, and selection of series by lesion site is not treated as a bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: The authors state that no meta-analysis was planned or done because of heterogeneity (p. 3259), yet the headline results are pooled shares made by adding patients across 17 heterogeneous, site-selected series (p. 3260; Table 4), with no weighting by study, no interval and no check of between-series differences. Judged as an inappropriate statistical combination. A reader who accepts the authors' label would score items 11, 12 and 15 as 'no meta-analysis'; the overall rating is unchanged either way (items 4, 7 and 13).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The two poor-quality series were kept on the statement that their data agreed with the others (pp. 3260–3261); no analysis without them, or without the site-selected series, is shown.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The only discussion of the impact of bias concerns the two poor-quality series and concludes there was none. The review notes that most series selected particular sites (most often the palate) or presentations and that many were non-consecutive, but states that no significant biases towards its objectives were identified (p. 3259) and never considers how this selection shapes the shares on which the classification rests.

Heterogeneity is cited as the reason for not pooling statistically (p. 3259), but differences between series in the share of each site (for example palate-selected against unselected series) are not examined or discussed.

Reporting bias is discussed only as a reason to exclude case reports (p. 3266); the selective publication of striking or site-specific series, which bears directly on the pooled shares, is not considered.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (p. 3266). The paper does not mention that one review author co-wrote an included series.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item fails: here items 7 (no list of excluded studies), 13 (selection bias of the series not considered in interpretation) and, by the project's reading, 4 (unjustified language limit) fail, with items 11 and 15 also judged 'no' and items 2 and 9 met in part. This is a judgment about how far the pooled site shares can be taken as an unbiased picture of where cocaine damages the nose, not about the paper's usefulness: the search was broad, selection was duplicated, and the tables let a reader see what each series contributed. Citable for: the counts of people with each site involved among the 127 people in the 17 published series (Table 4), described as counts in published case series, mostly selected; the near-universal septal involvement; and the absence of follow-up and cocaine-use data in the literature up to March 2021. Not citable for: how often snorting cocaine damages any part of the nose, the order in which damage spreads, or what happens after stopping.

key_findings.finding: From 2593 unique records and 190 full texts, 17 studies published 1989 to 2020 were included, all retrospective case series (OCEBM level 4); by the NHLBI tool 9 were rated good, 6 fair and 2 poor. Most lacked information on the comparability of patients, gave little or no follow-up, or were non-consecutive.
key_findings.locator: Results › Search results, 1st paragraph (p. 3259); Fig. 1 (p. 3260); Table 2 (p. 3261)

key_findings.finding: The 17 series held 127 people with CIMDL among 282 participants: 61 men and 44 women (sex not extractable for 22 people in two series), aged 22 to 66 years.

Share of the 127 people with each site involved: nasal septum 126 (99.2%); inferior turbinate or medial maxillary sinus wall 75 (59%); palate 38 (29.9%); ethmoid, middle or superior turbinate 29 (22.8%); lamina papyracea, orbit or skull base 10 (7.9%). The authors turn these into grades 1, 2a, 2b, 3 and 4.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 3264); Fig. 2 legend (p. 3265); denominator of 127 in Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 3260)
key_findings.note: The abstract (p. 3257) and results text (p. 3260) label 59% as the nasal floor and 29.9% as the inferolateral nasal wall; Table 4 and Fig. 2 give 59% to the inferior turbinate and medial maxillary wall and 29.9% to the palate. The table and figure are used here. These are counts added across mostly site-selected series, not rates among people who snort cocaine.

key_findings.finding: Septal perforation was found in all but one person; the exception, in Kuriloff and Kimmelman's series, had palatal damage with no septal involvement described. Individual lesion patterns could be reconstructed for only 18 people in four series; the other series reported only how many people had each site involved.

Changes to the outside of the nose were listed for 10 of 17 series, for example saddle nose (in 5 series) and collapse of the nasal pyramid (in 2 series). The authors could not relate the extent of internal damage to external deformity and suggest, without data, that longer and heavier use might worsen both.

Cocaine use was rarely described: some figure for duration in 11 of 17 series (2 to 30 years where given), frequency in 2, and continuing or stopped use in 8 series (editors' count from Table 3: 33 people, 18 continuing and 15 stopped); levamisole exposure in one study. The authors judge these data too sparse for any solid conclusion, let alone for relating use to the pattern of damage. (Counts recomputed and confirmed; 'solid' restored from p. 3265.)
key_findings.note: Series counts and the 33 people (18 and 15) are editors' counts from Table 3.

key_findings.finding: The review lacks longitudinal follow-up data: by its account only Trimarchi et al. (2003) gave sparse information on progression, which the authors say seems to confirm their hypothesis. The order of spread (septum, then lower and side walls, then ethmoid, then orbit or skull base) is the authors' hypothesis from the site shares, which they say needs prospective validation; the review reports no data on what happened to lesions after people stopped using cocaine. (The source does not say that no series reported this; it reports none. See 'missed' on Trimarchi et al., 2001.)

Surgical pathology, reported for some series, was mostly nonspecific: chronic inflammation, fibrosis or necrosis, with vasculitis-like changes (microabscesses in venule walls, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, thrombi) in two of the three Trimarchi series (2001 and 2003; Table 6 gives nonspecific findings for the 2017 series) and features suggesting IgG4 disease in one series. Histology could not be related to lesion extent or site.

The review does not test how CIMDL is told apart from other diseases. Its introduction says the pattern mimics, and is often indistinguishable from, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis and nasal non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and cites criteria by Seyer et al.: CIMDL is suspected when two of septal perforation, palatal perforation and lateral nasal wall destruction are present, with other diagnoses ruled out and toxicology screening.
No treatment, repair or outcome data are extracted or reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 1st paragraph (list of recorded items, p. 3259); Results (pp. 3259–3260)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and results text give the inferior third as nasal floor and inferolateral nasal wall at, respectively, 59% and 29.9%, while Table 4 and Fig. 2 give 59% to the inferior turbinate and medial maxillary sinus wall (grade 2a) and 29.9% to the palate (grade 2b).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whichever way the nasal floor is read, the abstract assigns 29.9% to the inferolateral wall, which Table 4 puts at 59%. Claims should take the site shares from Table 4 and Fig. 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The PRISMA figure says the 4133 records were identified on 1 December 2020; the text and Table 1 date the searches 4 March 2021 (the Table 1 counts add up to 4133, editors' arithmetic), and the review is said to have been conducted between 1 March and 15 August 2021.
reporting_issues.consequence: The search date, and therefore whether the PROSPERO registration preceded the search, cannot be settled from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says specimens were sent for pathology in 12 studies; Table 6 lists 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; two studies' pathology is either missing from the table or the text count is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Several counts in Table 6 exceed the number of people with CIMDL in the series: Subesinghe et al., 11 (6 people with CIMDL among 14); Trimarchi et al. 2001, 19, 24 and 25 (18 people); Trimarchi et al. 2003, 27 (25 people). The primary paper of Trimarchi et al. (2001) shows its figures are counts of biopsies (44 biopsies from 18 people), which the table does not say.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 6 mixes biopsy counts with patient counts; its numbers cannot be read as numbers of people. (The 2003 count of 22 does not exceed 25; 44 biopsies checked in the 2001 PDF.)

reporting_issues.issue: Series from the same groups may share patients, and the review does not say whether it checked: Trimarchi et al. 2001 (18 people) and 2003 (25) both have the age range 22 to 66, and all three Trimarchi series give 2 to 30 years of use; the two Colletti series (4 people each) give identical durations of use (5, 9, 10 and 10 years) and identical continuing or stopped status.
reporting_issues.consequence: If patients overlap, some people are counted twice in the 127 and the site shares are distorted.

reporting_issues.issue: Compared with the primary paper of Trimarchi et al. (2001), read in this session, Table 3 counts lateral nasal wall destruction as 3 (the primary paper: wall entirely absorbed in 3 clinically, eroded in 5 of 16 on imaging) and nasal floor erosion as 1 (primary: 4 of 16 on imaging), and includes 3 palatal perforations and 2 orbital pseudotumours (infections) that appeared only during follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled shares mix findings at first presentation with findings during follow-up and clinical with imaging counts, so they do not describe one time point or one method.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 2 (Marí et al.) is dated 2022, although the included studies are said to have been published between 1989 and 2020 and the search ran in March 2021.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in the reference list; the study cannot have been published after the search.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations say that in series without endoscopy anterior rhinoscopy was always coupled with CT or MR imaging, but Table 3 shows imaging for only part of some series (for example clinical examination in 8 people and CT in 3 in Green et al.; 5 and 3 in Kuriloff and Kimmelman) and no stated method for three series.
reporting_issues.consequence: Lesion sites were assessed less uniformly than the limitations paragraph implies, which may under-count deeper sites in some series.

reporting_issues.issue: Age is described as most often in the third or fourth decade in the results and as thirties or forties in the discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 2 gives ages mostly in the thirties and forties.
